To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the hierarchy of generalized logical consequence is the same as the Borel and alternation hierarchy, and that this hierarchy provides the framework of a unified theory of deduction, induction, and learning.
(1) The hierarchy of generalized logical consequence, (2) The hierarchy of Borel sets, (3) The hierarchy of quantifier alternations, (4) The hierarchy of learning capabilities, are all equivalent.

the hierarchy of generalized logical consequence is a generalization of the hierarchy of Borel classes, that it is a refinement of the hierarchy of quantifier alternations, and that the first level of the former hierarchy corresponds to finite learning, and the second level to learning in the limit.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of a logic which is at once inductive and deductive, and which provides a framework to unify deduction and induction.
the development of a general theory of deduction, induction, and learning, and its applications to artificial intelligence.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we have developed a general theory of learning and deduction, based on the notion of logical consequence, which encompasses classical first-order logic and the main inductive learning paradigms.
the theory we present here is a general framework in which deduction and induction are seen as two aspects of the same activity: the discovery and the use of knowledge.

our framework is a powerful tool to study the interrelations between the various aspects of scientific activity, and that this framework can provide a basis for the construction of a unified logical system which can be used as a general purpose tool for scientific reasoning.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have provided an answer to the following question: What is a theory of deduction and induction?
we have developed a general theory of inductive inference which is based on a general theory of logical inference.
we have developed a theory of "induction" which is as powerful as the "deduction" theory of classical logic.
The main takeaway from our work is that
inductive inference is not a special case of deduction, but rather a natural generalization of it, which can be embedded in a logical theory of discovery of truth, in the spirit of Popper.
the inductive capabilities of a system can be made explicit by a logical analysis of its behavior, and this is the basis for our inductive Prolog system.
learning is not just about deduction, and that the inductive nature should not be hidden behind the scene.
